_about: Oxygen in the air as a fraction of today's (1 = 21 %), 4 billion years to now: the envelope of the published reconstruction, read off the figure, the band being the point. Each point [year, value, low, high]; year is the store's astronomer's year. Made by tools/curves-deep-time.py.

source.citation: Lyons, T.W., Reinhard, C.T. & Planavsky, N.J. (2014), The rise of oxygen in Earth's early ocean and atmosphere, Nature 506, 307–315, figure 1; the Phanerozoic after Berner's GEOCARBSULF
source.note: values read from the figure's envelope, not from a table; the figure is drawn on a log axis and so is this. The points changed on the checkers' reading of 9 Oct 2026 (Plots-Deep-01.md): the rise across a hundred-thousandth of today's at 2,430 million years after Gumsley and others 2017; the coming and going until about 2,220 million years after Poulton and others 2021, drawn as a band that widens down to a millionth; the low edge from 2,000 to 800 million years after Planavsky and others 2014 (under 0.1 percent of today's); 300 million years (1.35, about 28 percent of the air) after Glasspool & Scott 2010 and Krause and others 2018; the step down at 252 million years, its size argued, after Berner 2006 and Krause and others 2018

howSure: A sketch of a published envelope. Before 2.4 billion years the air had almost none; the band across the Boring Billion is three orders of magnitude wide because that is how little is known; the Carboniferous high is the best-known point. Treat the line as the middle of the band, never as a reading.
_range: from and to are the store years (astronomer's years) the curve is meaningful between — its first and last points; minPoints is the fewest points a period must hold for the curve to be offered (Prompt-Build-Timeline-Stack.md, part 6, 10 Oct 2026)
